name: Crinoline and bustle dress
summary: The dress of the Second Empire: a vast bell skirt on a steel cage from 1856, then a bustle from 1870, in strong silk.

philosophy.core_thesis: The skirt is the dress: a steel cage and then a bustle carry yards of silk, and the couture house sets the shape each season.
design_principles: Carry the skirt on a cage of 12 to 20 steel hoops; the hem is up to 3 m across.
Cut the bodice close to the body, with a pointed front and a waist at 56 to 63 cm.
Use 10 to 20 m of silk for a day skirt, and up to 40 m for a ball gown.
In the 1870s, move the fullness to the back on a bustle pad of wire and horsehair.
Drape the overskirt in swags at the back, and add a train for evening.
Trim the skirt with flounces, pleats, bows and braid in rows.
Use the new strong dyes, so that the colour is deep and bright.
anti_patterns: A skirt that hangs straight from the waist
A soft waist with no stays
A bare, plain skirt with no trim
A short hem that shows the leg

silhouette.shape: In the 1860s, a fitted bodice sits over a very wide dome of skirt. In the 1870s and 1880s, the front is flat and the drape forms a shelf at the back.
silhouette.line: A low sloped shoulder, a pointed waist, and a skirt that grows into a bell, then moves back into a train.
silhouette.fit: Tight and boned at the torso; the skirt stands free of the legs on its cage or its bustle pad.
silhouette.proportion: The waist is 56 to 63 cm. The cage hem is up to 3 m across. The bustle shelf is 20 to 30 cm out from the back. The train is 30 to 60 cm long on the floor.
rules: Lace the corset first, then the cage or the pad, then the petticoats, then the dress.
Cut the skirt in gores so that it opens in a bell over the cage.
Draw the cloth up at the back into puffs and swags over the bustle.
Trim the hem in rows of flounces, braid or pleats.
Add gloves, a bonnet or a small hat, and a parasol.

fabrics.rule: Choose a silk with body: glazed taffeta and satin for the skirt, tulle for the ball gown, velvet for the bodice.

methods: cage of steel hoops on tapes
bustle pad of horsehair and wire
flounces and ruching sewn by hand and machine
construction.closures: Hooks and eyes down the front of the bodice; the skirt closes at the back with hooks and tapes.
construction.details: A pointed waist, a bertha collar on the ball gown, ribbon bows, rows of braid, a draped overskirt, and a train for evening.

surface.pattern: Plain strong colour, striped or shot silk, and rows of trim; a ball gown carries tulle and flowers.
surface.gloss: Taffeta and satin at 35–65 GU; velvet at 8–15 GU.
surface.wear: Silk splits along the fold and the weight of the skirt strains the seams; the dress is re-trimmed and re-cut with each change of line.

palette.strategy: Strong coloured silks from the new dyes for day; white and pale tones with flowers for the ball.

processes: haute couture to the measure of the client
hand finish of trim and flounces
making.scale: A court dressmaker makes the couture dress for the court. A local dressmaker makes a copy at a lower price. A factory makes the cage.
making.signs: A steel cage or bustle pad, a boned and lined bodice, deep hem trim, and a tape and hook fastening.

pieces.form: Day dress with a cage crinoline skirt in glazed silk
Ball gown with tiers of tulle over a silk skirt
Bustle dress with a draped overskirt and a train
Skirt of silk twill with rows of flounces
Fitted bodice of velvet with a pointed waist

canonical_works.work: The Empress Eugénie Surrounded by Her Ladies

evidence.title: Young woman in a long dress, jacket and crinoline, 1860s

emotion.target_response: A sense of display and wealth: the viewer sees a large, bright skirt and reads rank and effort.

use_cases: a period costume brief for a Victorian drama
a museum label for a 19th century gown
a fashion image prompt for a ball in Paris in 1865
a gown with a full tulle skirt for a bridal line
avoid_when: the brief is for easy movement
the brief is a 1920s or later dress
the brief wants a plain, light, soft dress

modifiers.how: Drop the cage, the corset and the train; cut a straight chemise at knee length.
Remove the cage, lift the waist under the bust, and use white muslin.

ornament_level.note: A day dress carries braid and flounces; a ball gown carries tulle, flowers and beads.
